name: Aaron Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and was promoted to junior manager of five risk reporting analysts in a large company last year. My bachelor's degree is in statistics and I use AI every day to draft charts, but I am still below the best managers at coaching people. The board pack and its ledger trail fill my mornings; what wears me out is discovering I fixed a chart without helping the analyst understand the error.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how is the household set up?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a nurse, our two children are at school, and we have a mortgage. I earn more than most managers at this level and we have about nine months of expenses in cash, with many similar jobs across the city. That lets me take some risks at work, though I don't want my analysts to pay for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my risk reporting team the AI note-taker is a useful pencil, not an auditor. We still owe the board a figure we can trace back to a ledger line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day for draft charts, but I am still learning how to manage five analysts without doing their work for them. I earn well, my partner's nursing wage is steady, and we have nine months of expenses saved against the mortgage and our two children's costs, so a plateau doesn't threaten us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll keep asking each analyst to show the source beside a risk chart and use AI only to draft the first caption. In the first year of a plateau, we'll leave our nine-month reserve alone and I will take the monthly peer-manager meeting to get better at giving feedback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about income, and a little embarrassed that coaching people takes me longer than cleaning a dataset. I'd like the quieter year to get better at the human part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What went wrong when you did an analyst's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Friday I rewrote a chart without telling Mira, and she spent an hour looking for a change she'd never made. I apologized and put her name back on the review note; my fast fix cost her trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use AI on that chart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a draft label, yes; the figures come from the team's ledger checks. A chart with no trail is just decoration for the board.

say: I'd say **AI captions** help, while every board figure still needs a ledger source.
I'd keep **analyst checks** beside risk charts rather than treat a draft as an audit.
think: Nine months saved and two steady wages make our **household secure** in a plateau.
I am still a **new manager** and sometimes harm trust by fixing an analyst's work myself.
do: Keep **source lines** beside risk charts and draft only the first caption with AI.
Attend **monthly peer meetings** to practise giving feedback instead of rewriting staff work.
feel: He feels **calm** about income and embarrassed by his slow growth as a manager.
S0.quote: A chart with no trail is just decoration for the board.
fieldNote: His **nine-month reserve** makes a mild AI change unthreatening to the household.
He admits a **specific management mistake** with Mira, separating technical speed from skill at leading people.

steps.text: Keep analyst source lines beside each board risk chart
Attend monthly peer-manager meetings to practise giving staff feedback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff forum Steady Disruption will take over first drafts of reports and checks, and the analysts must see how new targets are set. I'd ask management to publish the error log and discuss vacancies before claiming the tool has freed people for better work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, fewer reporting hours could mean one manager covers our five analysts and the neighboring team. I can operate the new systems, but I am the newest manager and not yet the best at the people side; the family reserve gives me time, not a guarantee of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll set up a trial on one quarterly risk pack with the staff forum watching the error log, and I'd ask HR for the actual hiring and vacancy numbers. In the first year of steady disruption, if the trial works, I'd configure the checking rules myself and seek a different internal reporting role only if one is posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about signing off on a smaller team. I want the staff to know the count before my name appears on a rollout slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would matter enough to stop the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missing debt covenant, which is a promise in a loan agreement, would stop it immediately; we have to show those to the board. A miss there could make a clean chart dangerously false.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why involve the staff forum when you can run the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the people being measured need to see the rules and challenge a wrong result. I have benefited from new tools, but I won't make colleagues carry a hidden score.

say: I'd ask for a **visible error log** and vacancy figures before calling the new reports a success.
I'd bring **analysts into target-setting** through the staff forum.
think: My **new manager post** may be combined with another team's as reporting hours fall.
Daily AI skill helps, but my **people management** is still weaker than some colleagues'.
do: Trial **one risk pack** with staff watching and stop if a loan promise disappears.
Configure **checking rules** if the trial works; seek a posted internal role if management posts combine.
feel: He feels **anxious** about owning a rollout that could shrink his team.
S1.quote: I have benefited from new tools, but I won't make colleagues carry a hidden score.
fieldNote: His **public staff voice** comes from a concrete risk: hidden targets could penalize analysts after automation.
His private worry is **manager consolidation**, despite strong cash and fluent tool use.

steps.text: Bring one risk-pack trial and error log to the staff forum
Configure automated checking rules if the one-pack trial works
Apply for another internal reporting role only if a post opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team AGI by 2028 could produce nearly every board report we make, and workers need a say in staffing before the decision is finished. I would insist that directors name the person who signs for a wrong covenant number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking work changes in 2028; robots around 2031 won't delay a reporting manager's risk. I could lose this new post, but nine months of savings, my partner's pay and plenty of local analyst jobs give us choices; the mortgage won't disappear just because we have options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll take our nine-month budget sheet to my partner and ask the staff forum to request a dated staffing meeting. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, I'd test its covenant checks against old signed reports if allowed; if the management layer goes, I'd apply for local audit analyst posts with pay that still covers mortgage and childcare, and keep paying the mortgage from our reserve while interviewing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, not overwhelmed. It would hurt to step back from management, but I would rather keep the house and let someone else have the title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check eligibility for job-loss support if I were cut, but I won't assume a payment exists in every place. I'd also ask the staff forum for written severance terms before any decision, because guessing won't cover a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner say about a step back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would care more about school pickup and a reliable wage than a manager label. I agree, though part of me would still feel I had failed the analysts I hired.

say: I'd seek a **dated staffing meeting** and a named signer for AGI-produced reports.
I'd tell the team **2028 thinking AI** reaches board reports before later robots.
think: My **new post** could go, even though nine months saved and local analyst roles offer choices.
The **mortgage and childcare** still need reliable wages if I step back from management.
do: Review the **nine-month budget** with my partner and seek staffing and severance terms now.
After 2028, test **old covenant reports** if allowed; seek audit analyst pay covering mortgage and childcare if cut.
Use the **nine-month reserve** for mortgage payments while interviewing if management ends.
feel: He feels **anxious** about losing management, but able to protect the household with a plan.
S2.quote: I would rather keep the house and let someone else have the title.
fieldNote: He correctly puts the **reporting shock in 2028**, with robots around 2031 irrelevant to his desk.
He would accept a **title step down** for mortgage-covering pay, while seeking collective staffing terms.

steps.text: Ask staff forum for dated staffing meeting and severance terms
Test AGI covenant checks on old signed reports after 2028 if allowed
Apply for local audit analyst posts if management ends and pay covers mortgage and childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the analysts AGI by 2031 gives us time to agree who is responsible for automated figures and to change how we work before jobs are removed. I'd ask the staff forum for a written plan that shows roles gained and lost each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me become better at leading people, but AGI can also coach and write reviews by 2031. My remaining value may be knowing when a team has been pushed past its limits; I can't assume that guarantees a post, and robots around 2034 offer no shelter to the reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next year, I'll use the company's existing AI to practise explaining risk figures to nontechnical colleagues and ask a mentor to critique my team reviews. In the first year after 2031, I'd apply for a posted risk governance role if one exists; otherwise I would use the local job market for a paid audit post before spending much of the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about how much of a manager's judgment could be copied. Five years gives me time to learn, but I still want a real vacancy at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the mentor actually see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give her a review where I rushed to fix someone's chart instead of asking why it failed. She would tell me whether I treated the analyst as a person or as another source of errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the governance role be automated too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My manager title cannot hide the fact that policy checks are thinking work too. I would only move if it paid enough and still required a person to answer for a decision, and I'd keep my eyes on openings outside the company.

say: I'd ask for **yearly role counts** and named responsibility for automated figures.
I'd tell analysts the **2031 runway** is time to negotiate the change, not just watch it.
think: Even team reviews and policy checks are **thinking work** AGI may perform in 2031.
Five years can improve my management, but it cannot **guarantee a post** in governance.
do: Use **current AI** to practise explaining risk figures and ask a mentor to critique my reviews next year.
Seek a **posted governance role** after 2031 only with viable pay and accountable human work; otherwise seek local audit posts.
feel: He feels **uneasy** about copied judgment while seeing time to build skill.
S3.quote: My manager title cannot hide the fact that policy checks are thinking work too.
fieldNote: He admits a **governance fallback** is thinking-exposed too, and asks for a real accountable vacancy.
His preparation combines **current AI practice** with feedback on how he treats analysts.

steps.text: Use current AI to practise explaining board risk figures next year
Apply for posted governance role after 2031 only if pay and human responsibility remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff forum AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to make rules for automated reports and careers that people can actually use. I would push for annual meetings where staff can challenge how performance is scored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 in 2036 and the children may be older, but I can't place my mortgage on a date when robots arrive around 2039; my desk changes when AGI does. Ten years could let me build a stronger record as a manager or move to another field, yet even careful governance work is still thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep my team on the board reporting calendar and join the staff forum's annual review of performance rules. This year I'd also enroll in a self-funded mediation certificate capped at 1,200; in the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd stay only if my job has accountable people decisions at viable pay, otherwise seek a local post before resigning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful and fairly secure because our savings buy time. I still worry about whether the analysts will have the same choices I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mediation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I argued with a colleague about an error score and realized I was trying to win rather than understand the working conditions behind it. I want to learn to hear both sides in a real meeting, not just ask AI for a nicer sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the annual meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want workers to see their own scores and challenge a wrong one with a person who can change it. A yearly meeting with no appeal route would be another slide deck.

say: I'd push for **annual staff meetings** on performance rules and appeal routes.
I'd say a decade should fund **usable careers**, not only polished automated reports.
think: At **53**, the mortgage still matters and robots in 2039 don't delay desk exposure.
Ten years could build my **management record** or allow another field, though governance remains thinking work.
do: Keep the **board calendar** and join annual staff review of performance rules this year.
Take a **self-funded mediation certificate** capped at 1,200; stay after 2036 only for viable accountable work.
feel: He feels **watchful but secure**, with concern for analysts who have fewer choices.
S4.quote: A yearly meeting with no appeal route would be another slide deck.
fieldNote: He brings **collective appeals** into the long-run plan rather than treating his cushion as everyone's solution.
Mediation is a **self-funded learning choice**, while any later governance or people role remains thinking-exposed.

steps.text: Keep five analysts on the board reporting calendar this year
Join annual staff forum review of performance scoring and appeals
Take self-funded mediation certificate costing at most 1,200
Apply locally after 2036 if accountable work or viable pay ends; keep job until written offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our board reports could become cheap before I have grown into the management part of my role. A dated staffing decision, open error logs, and a real appeal for staff scores would help us protect the people behind the numbers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets to correct a wrong performance score after an automated report goes to the board. A worker needs an appeal before a number becomes a verdict.

headlineQuote: A worker needs an appeal before a number becomes a verdict.
portrait: At **43**, Aaron leads five risk analysts and uses AI daily, but is still learning to coach rather than fix their work.
His **nine-month reserve**, high pay and local jobs allow risk, while a mortgage and children still matter.
He uses **staff forums** to seek visible error logs, vacancy counts and appeals alongside technical trials.
Fast AGI threatens his **new manager post**; longer runways let him improve people skills, with no guaranteed safe desk role.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cheapen board reporting before he becomes a strong manager.
whatWouldHelp: **Staffing dates**, open error logs and appeals for staff scores would protect his team during a shift.
